opus-5.5.text:
I think coding was the natural first domain because it has a property that's very rare: you get fast, cheap, mostly objective feedback. You write the code, you run the tests, and you know almost immediately whether it works. That tight loop is exactly what reinforcement learning and agentic systems need, and that's why we've seen such dramatic progress there in the last couple of years.

AI research sits right next to coding, but one level up. A big part of what researchers actually do day to day is coding: setting up experiments, writing training pipelines, debugging, running ablations, reading the curves, and deciding what to try next. Much of that is engineering work that's becoming automatable. So once agents can reliably write and run code, the obvious next question is: can they run the whole experimental loop? Can they propose a hypothesis, design the experiment, execute it, interpret the results, and iterate?

The reason this is such a big opportunity is leverage. If you automate a piece of ordinary software engineering, you get productivity gains in that one product. If you automate part of AI research, you speed up the process that produces the next generation of models, which then helps automate even more research. There's a compounding effect, a flywheel, that you don't get in most other domains.

That said, I want to be careful, because research isn't just execution. The hardest part is taste: knowing which problem matters, noticing when a weird result is actually a signal rather than noise, and having the intuition to abandon a direction or push through when everything looks bad. The feedback there is much sparser and noisier than a unit test. A paper might take months to show whether an idea was right, and sometimes years before the community recognizes it. So I see the near-term opportunity as automating the large, tedious middle of the research loop, freeing humans to focus on asking the right questions. The longer-term and much harder challenge is whether AI can develop real research taste. If it can, that changes everything. Personally, I'm very interested in understanding *why* these models work, not only making them work, because I think that understanding is what will eventually let us build systems that can do research in a deeper sense.

r001.rationale: The response says coding automation improves productivity in a product, but does not attribute high financial returns to replacing expensive human programming labor.

r002.rationale: The response describes the leverage and compounding effect of automating research, but does not identify the cost of researchers working on large models as a reason for high ROI.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the reason is actually pretty simple. If you look at what happened with coding over the last couple of years, the loop was very tight: the model writes code, the code either compiles or it doesn't, the tests pass or they fail, and you get a signal almost immediately. That's why coding agents got good so fast. AI research is, in a sense, the natural extension of that loop, just one level up.

When I do research, what am I actually doing most of the day? I read papers, I form a hypothesis, I write some code to test it, I launch experiments, I look at the curves, and then I decide what to try next. A huge fraction of that is already very close to what coding agents do today. The parts that feel "human," the intuition about what to try, are real, but they are also learnable, because the feedback is there. The experiment either works or it doesn't. The loss goes down or it doesn't. So you have a verifiable signal, which is exactly the condition under which these systems improve quickly.

The second reason is leverage. If an agent writes a better web app, you get a better web app. If an agent discovers a better optimizer, or a better data mixture, or a better architecture trick, that improvement goes back into the next model, and the next model becomes a better researcher. That compounding is what makes it the biggest opportunity, not just a convenient one. In coding you have a product. In research you have a flywheel.

And the third thing, honestly, is that the bottleneck in the field right now is not compute alone, it's researcher attention. There are thousands of small ideas that nobody has time to try. Most of them fail, a few of them matter, and we currently find the ones that matter by having very smart people grind through the space by hand. If you can automate even the lower-level part of that, the ablations, the hyperparameter sweeps, the "does this trick survive at scale" question, then the humans move up to deciding which directions are worth exploring at all. That's the same transition we saw with coding, where people stopped writing boilerplate and started thinking about architecture. I expect research to follow the same path, and I think it will happen faster than people expect, because the infrastructure for it, the agents and the evaluation loops, is already mostly here.

r001.rationale: The response explains coding automation through fast feedback from compilation and tests, but does not attribute its financial return to replacing expensive human programming labor.

r002.rationale: It cites researcher attention as a bottleneck and describes automation's leverage, but does not identify the cost of researchers working on large models as a source of large financial return.

astra-6.text:
I think coding is a natural first step because you have a relatively clear feedback loop: you write a program, run it, and check whether it works. But in AI research, writing code is only one part of the process. You also have to decide what question to ask, design an experiment, interpret the results, and figure out what to try next.

If an AI system can do that whole loop, it becomes much more than a coding assistant. For example, when a training run fails to improve performance, the system needs to ask: Is there a bug? Is the optimization wrong? Or is the hypothesis itself wrong? Then it needs to design an experiment that distinguishes those possibilities. That ability to turn an uncertain result into a useful next step is central to research.

The opportunity is especially interesting because improvements in AI research can help us build better AI systems, which can then help with further research. Of course, that doesn’t mean progress automatically becomes unlimited. Compute, experiment time, and the quality of evaluation still matter. But it could substantially shorten the cycle between having an idea and finding out whether it works. That’s why I see it as a major next step after coding.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts coding with AI research but does not attribute coding automation’s financial return to replacing expensive programming labor.

r002.rationale: It mentions compute and experiment time as constraints, but does not identify the cost of researchers working on large models as a reason automation could yield a large return on investment.

sol-6.1.text:
I think coding is one part of a much bigger loop. In research, you start with a question, formulate a hypothesis, design an experiment, implement it, look at the results, and then decide what to try next. Coding tools help with implementation, but there’s an opportunity to automate more of that whole process.

AI research is especially interesting because many experiments happen entirely in a digital environment. You can change an algorithm, run training, evaluate the model, and get feedback. Of course, that feedback can be noisy, and choosing the right experiment is often harder than writing the code. But that’s precisely where a research agent could become valuable: connecting results to the next hypothesis, rather than just executing a task someone has already specified.

And there’s a compounding effect. If AI can help us develop better AI, then those better systems can help us do research more effectively. I don’t think that means scientific breakthroughs suddenly become automatic. The near-term opportunity is to make the research cycle faster and let people explore ideas they otherwise wouldn’t have time to test.

r001.rationale: The response describes coding tools as helping with implementation, but does not attribute coding automation’s financial return to replacing expensive programming labor.

r002.rationale: The response says automating research could speed up the research cycle, but does not mention the cost of researchers working on large models or connect that cost to return on investment.
